newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban claim gains, tell foes to surrender.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban claim gains, tell foes to surrender.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia said its forces had made fresh gains in opposition-held territory on Tuesday and demanded that its foes surrender.

The Taleban said they had captured the Shibar Pass in central Afghanistan that leads to the opposition-held city of Bamiyan and commands a route to the north. A spokesman for the opposition Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat group denied the claim.

Maulvi Wakil Ahmad, a senior Taleban official based in the southern city of Kandahar, said forces in revolt against ethnic Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum had seized Kunduz and Sar-i-Pul, the capitals of Kunduz and Jowzjan provinces.
There was no independent confirmation of the latest reported advances by troops led by dissident General Abdul Malik, who launched a Taleban-backed uprising against Dostum on Monday.
Malik, governor of Faryab province, is the brother of Rasul Pahlivan, a senior Dostum commander assassinated last year.
The Taleban's supreme leader, Mullah Mohammad Omar, told all opposition leaders to stop fighting or face Islamic justice.

"All those fighting the Taleban should surrender immediately," Omar said in a statement from his Kandahar headquarters. "Those who surrender voluntarily face no threat and their lives and property will be protected.
"Those who are forced to surrender by the Taleban will face Islamic courts," the statement, carried by the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) service, said.
Omar said opposition leaders Dostum and Ahmad Shah Masood should "cease further bloodshed in Afghanistan and stop fooling the people".

"They must give themselves up to the Islamic (Taleban) government. If they continue spilling blood and wasting public funds, there will be a decision against them in an Islamic court," the Taleban leader declared.
He told neighbouring countries to keep out of Afghanistan's internal affairs "at this sensitive time" or take responsibility for what he called "the dangerous consequences".
Taleban radio said in a broadcast from Kabul on Monday night that the Islamic militia was advancing on Faryab after breaking through Dostum's defences. It gave no details.
But an opposition spokesman said on Tuesday that Taleban forces had not yet entered Faryab and negotiations were continuing to keep Malik in the opposition alliance.

"So far the Taleban have not entered Faryab. We are trying to solve the problem between Malik and Dostum. We have already started this," opposition spokesman Dr Abdullah (one name) told Reuters by telephone from the north.
AIP said on Monday Dostum seemed to have kept control of Mazar-i-Sharif, but there has been no word on his whereabouts.
Independent sources confirmed a report that Malik had captured former Herat provincial governor Ismail Khan, who had been fighting the Taleban in northwestern Afghanistan.
It was not immediately clear whether Khan would be handed over to the Taleban, who forced him to flee from Herat and take refuge in neighbouring Iran in September 1995.
